title: Echoes Without Evidence: Media Coverage, Information Quality, and Claim Genealogy During the PHP2Shell Incident (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619)
content: Public information on vulnerabilities translates technical findings into statistics de-scribing how common a vulnerability is, how many were found, exploited, and actions taken. Here we present a systematic literature review of PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618/CVE-2026-109619) alongside its media coverage [CERT-EU, Tzadik]. We performed a systematic retrospective information analysis on 60 English documents. We used a systematic claim-type coding scheme to separate how informative each claim is, who is taking credit, whether claims are independently verified, and how much information was actually given in the original source. Claims were coded by one individual; any disagreement on these fields was adjudicated by a second individual. Results: Of the 60 documents 25 included the ∼70% statis-tic for how common PHP was (20 were usage share statistics, 8 were vulnerability/exposure). 28 included AI in the discovery (19 were also human). 22 referenced the MadPot honeypot (21 of these were attempts). 22 contained claims about exploitation (2 were attempts, 11 were honeypot exploitation, 4 were exploitation on real systems, 5 had inadequate information, 0 had exploitation in production). 12 contained claims attributed to Unit 42 (8 had withdrawn claims). We demonstrate that we need to consider how many claims there are, what qualifiers were added, and how much evidence there was. We also demonstrate that multiple publications do not mean independent verification, and whilst corrections were published they may not have been widely shared. The scheme, data dictionary and analysis scripts have been made available so the descriptive findings can be replicated computationally.
